# Fly.io Security & Compliance Questionnaire

Last updated: 2026-10-26

These are Fly.io’s standing answers to the security, privacy, data-protection and contracting questions customers and their vendor-review tools ask most. They describe the platform as it is operated today and are kept current by the Fly.io security team. The same answers are available as a spreadsheet from the Trust Center in the Fly.io dashboard, alongside the DPA, BAA and SOC 2 report.

Questions not covered here go to [compliance@fly.io](mailto:compliance@fly.io ""). Related documents: [Sub-processors](https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/ ""), [Privacy Statement](https://fly.io/legal/privacy-policy/ ""), [Data Privacy Framework notice](https://fly.io/legal/data-privacy-framework/ ""), [Security at Fly.io](https://fly.io/docs/security/security-at-fly-io/ "").

## [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-corporate-it-security) CORPSEC: Corporate/IT Security

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-1-which-third-party-audits-and-attestations-has-fly-io-obtained) CORPSEC-1: Which third party audits and attestations has Fly.io obtained?

**SOC2.** Fly.io is compliant with SOC2, via a SOC2 Type 2 audit conducted by Aprio. Our current report covers the period August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 and was issued on September 3, 2026, and we maintain the audit on an annual cycle. The report is available under NDA from the Trust Center in the Fly.io dashboard to organizations with the Compliance Package (see COMPLIANCE-16 and COMPLIANCE-31).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-2-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-information-security-policy) CORPSEC-2: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed information security policy?

**Yes.** A reviewed information security policy is a SOC2 requirement. We do not make our security policy available to customers (we may someday!). Our most recent SOC2 report includes audited details of our policy. Our information security policy is not a boilerplate we downloaded from the Internet.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-3-are-fly-io-employees-required-to-complete-security-awareness-training) CORPSEC-3: Are Fly.io employees required to complete security awareness training?

**Yes.** Security awareness training is a SOC2 requirement.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-4-does-fly-io-rely-on-single-sign-on-an-identity-provider-idp-or-other-source-of-authentication-truth-for-internal-applications) CORPSEC-4: Does Fly.io rely on single sign-on, an identity provider (IdP), or other source of authentication truth for internal applications?

**Yes.** We have two sources of authentication truth, layered (employees need both). Our primary IdP is Google’s IdP, and we additionally use Github for access to some development resources; for instance, access to a development server requires both valid Google-backed identity, AND valid Github-backed identity. Wherever possible, third-party services we rely on are linked to Google’s identity services. Internal services we ourselves build rely on Google identity for login (access to our internal networks does not grant automatic access to our internal services; the network is not “trusted”).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-5-how-does-fly-io-secure-account-access-to-services-not-enrolled-in-single-sign-on) CORPSEC-5: How does Fly.io secure account access to services not enrolled in single sign-on?

**1Password.** Our last-resort secret management system is 1Password, which is configured into a series of vaults based on need-to-know, with hazmat secrets confined to a small number of employees.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-6-are-fly-io-employees-required-to-use-multi-factor-authentication-2fa-mfa) CORPSEC-6: Are Fly.io employees required to use multi-factor authentication (2FA, MFA)?

**Yes.** We enforce MFA for Google and Github accounts; Google accounts must use phishing-resistant MFA, and we disallow SMS MFA.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-7-how-does-fly-io-physically-secure-its-offices) CORPSEC-7: How does Fly.io physically secure its offices?

**N/A.** We don’t have offices; our company is fully remote. We thus don’t have line items for physical security, guest checkin, etc. By implication: we don’t have security practices that rely on access to a trusted location or trusted networks.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-8-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-incident-response-plan) CORPSEC-8: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed incident response plan?

**Yes.** A reviewed IR plan is a SOC2 requirement. We don’t make our IR plan available to customers, but some audited details of it are included in our SOC2 report. Our IR policy is not a boilerplate we downloaded from the Internet, and it does document an escalation chain with named incident managers and last-resort 24/7 contacts.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-9-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-access-management-policy) CORPSEC-9: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed access management policy?

**Yes.** A reviewed access management policy is a SOC2 requirement. We don’t make our access management policy available to customers, but some audited details of it are included in our SOC2 report.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-10-does-fly-io-require-employees-to-routinely-change-passwords) CORPSEC-10: Does Fly.io require employees to routinely change passwords?

**No.** Scheduled password changes was a faulty best practice in the 1990s when it was devised, and is now specifically not recommended by NIST. Note that we require MFA for all our services, enforced via an SSO IdP.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-11-does-fly-io-enforce-password-complexity-rules-for-employee-accounts) CORPSEC-11: Does Fly.io enforce password complexity rules for employee accounts?

**Yes.** Password complexity rules are a SOC2 requirement. We enforce password complexity via policy rules in Google’s identity system.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-12-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-process-for-securely-transmitting-data-between-employees-and-partners) CORPSEC-12: Does Fly.io have a documented process for securely transmitting data between employees and partners?

**Yes.** We rely on Google Drive for document exchange in the normal case; in special cases, we have documented policies (see DATA) for exchanging secrets and sensitive documents securely outside of Google, using encrypted transports.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#corpsec-13-does-fly-io-have-a-security-team-and-a-security-officer) CORPSEC-13: Does Fly.io have a security team and a security officer?

**Yes.** We have a security team, 24/7 contacts for security, and a full-time, dedicated security lead (our Security Officer).

## [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-production-fleet-security) INFRASEC: Production/Fleet Security

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-1-does-fly-io-monitor-its-systems-for-vulnerabilities-and-if-so-how-and-on-what-cadence) INFRASEC-1: Does Fly.io monitor its systems for vulnerabilities, and, if so, how and on what cadence?

**Yes.** Basic vulnerability management is a part of our SOC2 attestation. We monitor vulnerability feeds for our major infrastructure components (principally: Linux). We do regular automated scanning of our production systems for new exposures. The core of our vulnerability management strategy is not to deploy much 3rd party code on our systems; virtually all of our exposed attack surface is code we ourselves have written.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-2-does-fly-io-control-access-to-production-systems) INFRASEC-2: Does Fly.io control access to production systems?

**Tailscale and Teleport.** Access to any of our internal services or production fleet requires a Tailscale login. Tailscale in turn requires a valid fly.io Google account (see CORPSEC). Tailscale is configured with default-deny ACLs; explicit group membership is required to access a production server. Access to Tailscale DOES NOT confer access to production hosts; we control SSH access to our prod fleet with Teleport. We run Teleport internally; it’s not a hosted service. Access to Teleport implies Tailscale access. Teleport requires a valid Github SSO login, and membership in an appropriate group for the host being accessed. We maintain transcript-level logs of every SSH access to our fleet.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-3-does-fly-io-have-a-separate-development-environment-for-testing-and-staging-new-code-changes) INFRASEC-3: Does Fly.io have a separate development environment for testing and staging new code changes?

**Yes.** A separate development environment is part of our SOC2 attestation. We run separate physical hosts for dev access. Some CI/CD testing in development is done on Google’s GCP cloud or AWS; no part of that testing involves access to our services in any form (it’s just headless unit testing).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-4-what-public-clouds-does-fly-io-use-to-deliver-services-and-how-are-they-used) INFRASEC-4: What public clouds does Fly.io use to deliver services, and how are they used?

**AWS and GCP.** We make minimal use of both AWS and GCP. We use AWS for RDS, for the database that backs our API service, and for S3, where we store backups and built artifacts. We use GCP for some CI/CD testing.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-5-how-are-physical-machines-operated-by-fly-io-secured) INFRASEC-5: How are physical machines operated by Fly.io secured?

**Major Data Centers.** Our physical servers are hosted in large commercial data centers operated by our hosting providers - currently CacheNetworks (CacheFly), DataPacket, Latitude.sh, NetActuate and Vultr. These facilities have extensive physical security controls. Our current provider list is published at [https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/](https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/). Employees at Fly.io do not, as a rule, have direct physical access to our production servers.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-6-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-vulnerability-management-process) INFRASEC-6: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed vulnerability management process?

**Yes.** A vulnerability management process is part of our SOC2 attestation.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-7-does-fly-io-have-a-standard-build-for-production-hosts-and-how-is-it-managed) INFRASEC-7: Does Fly.io have a standard build for production hosts, and how is it managed?

**Yes.** A standard build process is part of our SOC2 attestation. We use a system called FCM (“Fly Configuration Management”) to establish known-good builds on our fleet; it runs periodically against all hosts. That build includes a custom build of the Linux kernel, and locked versions of our (minimal) third-party dependencies and telemetry. FCM is managed in git, with protected branches and mandatory reviews.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-8-how-does-fly-io-secure-deployments-of-software-and-updates-of-its-own-code-to-hosts) INFRASEC-8: How does Fly.io secure deployments of software and updates of its own code to hosts?

**CI/CD.** CI/CD is part of our SOC2 attestation. Our CI/CD system uses our own compute services (“Fly Machines”) to run builds; our platform injects the secrets required to certify builds and deliver them to S3; our deployment tooling extracts these certified builds from S3 to deploy them. This tooling is all managed in git, with protected banches and mandatory reviews. Fly.io developers do not, as a general rule, have direct access to the secrets required to push certified builds. Out-of-process changes are logged, with transcript-level SSH audit history.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-9-does-fly-io-deploy-antivirus-or-anti-malware-agents-on-production-fleet-machines) INFRASEC-9: Does Fly.io deploy antivirus or anti-malware agents on production fleet machines?

**No.** You wouldn’t want us running janky AV products on our production fleet, where nothing runs (outside of customer VMs) other than software we’ve certified.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-10-does-fly-io-deploy-data-loss-prevention-software-on-production-fleet-machines) INFRASEC-10: Does Fly.io deploy data-loss prevention software on production fleet machines?

**No.** You wouldn’t want us running janky DLP products on our production fleet; further, data in transit on the Fly.io platform is end-to-end encrypted, so there’s generally nothing for DLP products to find social security numbers in.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-11-does-fly-io-use-network-firewalls-to-protect-production-hosts) INFRASEC-11: Does Fly.io use network firewalls to protect production hosts?

**Yes.** Every host in our fleet has kernel IP filtering, with access rules defined by FCM (see above), managed in git with protected branches and mandatory reviews. We expose virtually nothing to the public Internet outside of the Anycast services that our own software supports. Our internal VPN is managed by Tailscale, with port-level ACLs; for the most part, no services are exposed on our Tailscale network besides Teleport-controlled SSH and services with Google-identity-backed logins.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-12-does-fly-io-monitor-its-fleet-for-security-events) INFRASEC-12: Does Fly.io monitor its fleet for security events?

**Yes.** Security monitoring is a baseline SOC2 requirement. We offer log retention, monitoring, search, and forwarding as a platform feature; the same capabilities back our own operational logging, which runs on VictoriaLogs that we host ourselves. Security detection is a separate pipeline: cloud audit logs (AWS CloudTrail), identity provider and workspace events, source control, password manager and tailnet audit events, tailnet network flows, employee device telemetry and internal tool logs feed Wazuh on AWS OpenSearch, with automated triage in front of the alert stream and long-term retention. It does not ingest customer application logs. The ingestion path carries a freshness check that alerts us if it stops receiving data.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#infrasec-13-is-traffic-in-the-fly-io-production-environment-encrypted) INFRASEC-13: Is traffic in the Fly.io production environment encrypted?

**Yes.** Transit encryption is a part of our SOC2 attestation. We run a WireGuard mesh between every node in our fleet; there is no routable addressing outside of our WireGuard network, and it would take substantial effort to communicate between any two hosts in our network without encryption. We further use mTLS (TLS with client certificates) to control access to certain internal services.

## [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#software-software-security-and-vulnerability-management) SOFTWARE: Software Security and Vulnerability Management

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#software-1-does-fly-io-undergo-periodic-third-party-software-penetration-testing) SOFTWARE-1: Does Fly.io undergo periodic third-party software penetration testing?

**Yes.** Periodic penetration tests are part of our SOC2 attestation; we commission an independent third-party test annually, scoped to our production platform. Our most recent test was conducted by Calif Security on 13 July 2026. Prior engagements were with IncludeSecurity and Atredis Partners. We do not distribute penetration test reports to customers, or to parties downstream of customers - the report describes attack paths and unremediated lower-severity findings on infrastructure shared by every Fly.io customer, so circulating it raises risk for every tenant rather than only the party asking. This is the same posture the major public clouds take. Our SOC2 report is the artifact built for redistribution, and it is where an independent auditor confirms we run an effective testing program. A signed attestation letter stating the date, firm, scope and severity outcome is available on request from [compliance@fly.io](mailto:compliance@fly.io).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#software-2-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-change-management-process) SOFTWARE-2: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed change management process?

**Yes.** A reviewed change management policy is a SOC2 requirement. We don’t make our change management policy available to customers, but some audited details of it are included in our SOC2 report. Per SOC2 requirements, all changes to our software occur via PRs; our repositories have protected branches, and we have mandatory review of changes.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#software-3-does-fly-io-review-software-changes-for-vulnerabilities) SOFTWARE-3: Does Fly.io review software changes for vulnerabilities?

**Yes.** Our security team reviews flagged PRs for security issues, and we undergo periodic 3rd-party penetration testing.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#software-4-does-fly-io-manage-the-security-of-dependencies-and-the-software-supply-chain) SOFTWARE-4: Does Fly.io manage the security of dependencies and the software supply chain?

**Cargo, Go Modules, Dependabot.** We maintain locked versions of all our dependencies. Our principle languages are Rust, Go, Elixir, and Ruby; Rust and Go both have first-class supply chain security features (locked dependencies, published hashes); we use Github’s Dependabot tracking for our Ruby API dependencies (we minimize new Ruby dependencies).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#software-5-does-fly-io-build-software-written-in-c-or-c) SOFTWARE-5: Does Fly.io build software written in C or C++?

**No.** Everything we build is memory-safe, with very carefully managed exceptions for major dependencies like SQLite.

## [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-encryption-data-at-rest-privacy-and-data-handling) DATA: Encryption, Data at Rest, Privacy, and Data Handling

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-1-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-data-classification-policy) DATA-1: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed data classification policy?

**Yes.** A reviewed data classification policy is a SOC2 requirement. We do not make our data classification policy available to customers. Our most recent SOC2 report includes audited details of our policy. Our data classification policy is not a boilerplate we downloaded from the Internet; it includes rules for storage, transmission, and sharing of data at each level of classification we manage.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-2-is-customer-data-segregated-from-other-customers-and-how) DATA-2: Is customer data segregated from other customers, and how?

**Yes.** We don’t operate multi-tenant storage systems for customer application data; if you’re storing data, you’re using provisioned block devices allocated specifically for your application (“Fly Volumes”, the basis for “Fly Postgres”).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-3-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-privacy-policy) DATA-3: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed privacy policy?

**Yes.** A reviewed privacy policy is a SOC2 requirement; it’s available on our website at [https://fly.io/legal/privacy-policy/](https://fly.io/legal/privacy-policy/). See COMPLIANCE-1 for our controller and processor roles and COMPLIANCE-15 for data subject requests.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-4-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-data-retention-policy) DATA-4: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed data retention policy?

**Yes.** A reviewed retention policy is a SOC2 requirement. We do not make our retention policy available to customers. Our legal counsel drafted our retention policy; we seek to minimize retention to the extent allowed by law and security requirements.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-5-does-fly-io-have-a-documented-reviewed-bc-dr-policy) DATA-5: Does Fly.io have a documented, reviewed BC/DR policy?

**Yes.** A reviewed BC/DR is a SOC2 requirement. We do not make our BC/DR policy available to customers. It includes provisions for how to maintain business continuity in the event a comet hits any one of us, up to and including our CEO. We exercise it: our most recent test was a restore-and-validate drill of our production control-plane database, conducted 2 June 2026 with recorded timings and an evidence packet.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-6-is-fly-io-customer-data-backed-up) DATA-6: Is Fly.io customer data backed up?

**Yes.** We take daily snapshots of Fly Volumes and store them in AWS S3 in the United States (us-east-1), regardless of the volume’s region. Snapshots of encrypted volumes (the default) are stored as encrypted block data. Retention is 5 days by default and configurable from 1 to 60 days, and automatic snapshots can be disabled per volume. Managed Postgres backups are stored in an AWS S3 bucket in the same geographic area as the cluster. See COMPLIANCE-6 for where data is held.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-7-is-customer-data-at-rest-in-fly-io-encrypted-and-does-that-encryption-apply-as-well-to-backups) DATA-7: Is customer data at rest in Fly.io encrypted, and does that encryption apply as well to backups?

**Yes.** All of our backups are encrypted; Fly Volumes are, by default, block-level encrypted with per-customer keys.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#data-8-when-a-machine-is-suspended-how-is-the-memory-snapshot-protected-where-is-it-stored-and-when-is-it-deleted) DATA-8: When a Machine is suspended, how is the memory snapshot protected, where is it stored, and when is it deleted?

**Encrypted, host-local, deleted on stop.** A suspend snapshot (the Machine’s memory and CPU state) is written only to a dedicated LUKS (dm-crypt) volume on the host that runs the Machine, in the Machine’s region. The volume is formatted at every host boot with a random key held only in host memory and never written to disk; the key is per host and separate from volume encryption keys. The snapshot is never replicated to another host, to object storage, or to a backup. It is single-use: the usable marker is removed before the snapshot is loaded, so it cannot be resumed twice. It is deleted when the Machine is stopped, updated, destroyed, or migrated (a migrated Machine cold-boots on the new host; the snapshot is not transferred), on host reboot (the volume is reformatted with a new key), and by a host cleanup that removes snapshot files older than two hours when the snapshot volume runs low on space. Deletion unlinks the files on the encrypted volume; remaining ciphertext is unrecoverable once the host key is discarded at reboot. Customers can discard a Machine’s snapshot without destroying it by stopping the suspended Machine.

## [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-privacy-data-protection-and-contracting) COMPLIANCE: Privacy, Data Protection, and Contracting

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-1-which-legal-entity-is-the-contracting-party-and-is-fly-io-a-data-controller-or-a-data-processor) COMPLIANCE-1: Which legal entity is the contracting party, and is Fly.io a data controller or a data processor?

**Fly.io, Inc..** The contracting party for all Fly.io services is Fly.io, Inc. For the data in your applications we act as a processor on your instructions, and you are the controller. For your account and billing data we are the controller. If you are yourself a processor, the DPA’s Article 28 terms apply down the chain (Article 28(4)).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-2-do-you-offer-an-article-28-data-processing-agreement-on-which-plans-and-how-do-we-sign-it) COMPLIANCE-2: Do you offer an Article 28 Data Processing Agreement, on which plans, and how do we sign it?

**Yes, every plan.** Yes. The DPA is available to every organization on every plan, self-service from the Trust Center in the Fly.io dashboard. It is pre-signed by Fly.io and becomes binding when your signed copy comes back to us. It covers all Fly.io products, including Sprites and Managed Postgres, and can be re-executed under a new entity name from the Trust Center. An individual customer with no legal entity signs in their own full name.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-3-what-is-your-international-transfer-mechanism-for-personal-data-from-the-eu-uk-and-switzerland-to-the-us) COMPLIANCE-3: What is your international transfer mechanism for personal data from the EU, UK and Switzerland to the US?

**Data Privacy Framework.** Fly.io, Inc. is certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, including the UK Extension, and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (participant 9027, originally certified 9 August 2024; see [https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/participant/9027](https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/participant/9027)). Transfers to us rest on that adequacy decision. For any transfer the DPF does not cover, the DPA embeds the 2021 EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Module 2, controller to processor) as Annex 2.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-4-for-uk-transfers-do-you-use-the-idta-or-the-uk-addendum-to-the-sccs) COMPLIANCE-4: For UK transfers, do you use the IDTA or the UK Addendum to the SCCs?

**UK Extension to the DPF.** The UK Extension to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework is our transfer mechanism for UK personal data, so neither instrument is needed for transfers to Fly.io. The standard DPA does not embed the IDTA or the UK Addendum. Section 13.4 of the DPA lets you add the UK Addendum on 30 days’ written notice if your own analysis requires it.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-5-we-are-a-processor-not-a-controller-do-you-offer-module-3-sccs) COMPLIANCE-5: We are a processor, not a controller. Do you offer Module 3 SCCs?

**Not needed.** Our DPA contains the Module 2 (controller to processor) clauses only. Because Fly.io is DPF-certified, transfers to us are covered by an adequacy decision and are not Restricted Transfers under the DPA (definition 1.1.11), so the SCCs do not trigger regardless of your role. Your own Article 28 obligations to your controller flow down through the DPA.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-6-where-is-our-data-physically-held-does-any-of-it-leave-the-region-we-choose) COMPLIANCE-6: Where is our data physically held? Does any of it leave the region we choose?

**Your regions, with exceptions.** Your application data, meaning your Machines and the volumes attached to them, stays in the regions you deploy to. Some data is held in the United States regardless of region: control plane data (accounts, organizations, app and release configuration, secrets), volume snapshots (stored as LUKS-encrypted block data in AWS S3 us-east-1; automatic snapshots can be disabled per volume), and container images. Managed Postgres backups are stored in an AWS S3 bucket in the same geographic area as the cluster. See DATA-6 for backups.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-7-is-a-regions-hardware-physically-located-in-that-country-and-who-are-your-hosting-providers) COMPLIANCE-7: Is a region’s hardware physically located in that country, and who are your hosting providers?

**Yes.** Yes. A Fly.io region is a physical datacenter location in the named city. Our worker hosts, where Machines and volumes run, are leased from CacheNetworks (CacheFly), DataPacket, Latitude.sh and Vultr; NetActuate hosts our gateways and edges. All of them are on our published sub-processor list at [https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/](https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/). See also INFRASEC-5.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-8-can-tls-be-terminated-only-inside-the-eu-can-request-bodies-be-decrypted-at-an-edge-outside-the-eu) COMPLIANCE-8: Can TLS be terminated only inside the EU? Can request bodies be decrypted at an edge outside the EU?

**No per-app edge restriction.** Fly Proxy terminates TLS at whichever edge Anycast routes the connection to, normally the edge nearest the client. There is no per-app restriction on which edges accept traffic, and nothing is stored at the edge. If plaintext must stay inside your Machine, expose a raw TCP service without the tls handler and terminate TLS in your application.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-9-where-is-your-sub-processor-list-and-how-are-we-told-about-changes) COMPLIANCE-9: Where is your sub-processor list, and how are we told about changes?

**fly.io/legal/sub-processors.** Our sub-processor list, with each vendor’s location and activity, is published at [https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/](https://fly.io/legal/sub-processors/) and carries a dated changelog. Under section 6.3 of the DPA we update the list at least 30 days before a new or replacement sub-processor processes customer personal data; the web page is the notice. You may object in writing on data-protection grounds, and if we cannot resolve the objection you may terminate the affected service.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-10-do-you-use-ai-vendors-and-do-they-see-our-application-data-or-logs) COMPLIANCE-10: Do you use AI vendors, and do they see our application data or logs?

**No training; internal inference only.** Fly.io does not train, fine-tune or improve AI or machine-learning models on customer data. Anthropic and OpenAI are listed on our sub-processor page and are used only by Fly.io’s internal tooling, for inference, under commercial API terms that prohibit training on submitted content (Anthropic: “Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services”; OpenAI: “OpenAI will not use Customer Content to develop or improve the Services, unless Customer explicitly agrees”). We never send the contents of your volumes or databases, or the bodies of requests to your applications, to an AI vendor. During support and abuse investigations the data that can be processed is account and organization metadata, support ticket text, and platform log lines, which include whatever your application writes to stdout; for Managed Postgres, a cluster’s Postgres logs and the results of a read-only diagnostic query an operator runs during an investigation. Both vendors process API requests in the United States. There is no per-customer setting to exclude an account from this processing; the control on your side is not writing personal data to stdout. See COMPLIANCE-22 for other sub-processors.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-11-how-long-do-you-keep-our-data-after-termination) COMPLIANCE-11: How long do you keep our data after termination?

**30 days; backups within 90.** Under Section 10 of the DPA, customer data is deleted within 30 days of the end of services (10.1), returned first on request (10.2), with written certification within 60 days (10.4). In practice deleting an app or organization removes its Machines, volumes and secrets immediately. Annex I.B’s 90 days is the outer bound for residual encrypted backup copies: volume snapshots age out on their configured retention (5 days by default, 60 at most, disableable per volume) and Managed Postgres backups on theirs, and no copy persists past 90 days. Section 10.3 covers only records law requires us to keep.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-12-what-do-you-log-about-our-application-and-its-users-including-visitor-ip-addresses-for-how-long-and-can-we-shorten-or-export-it) COMPLIANCE-12: What do you log about our application and its users, including visitor IP addresses, for how long, and can we shorten or export it?

**7 days.** Application stdout and stderr are searchable for 7 days; this retention is fixed and there is no customer setting to shorten it. Fly Proxy records the app id, SNI hostname and request path on errors; client IP addresses of inbound requests are not retained in our log store. Metrics are retained for about 15 days. You can ship a copy of your logs to your own sink with fly-log-shipper, which does not remove our copy. Website analytics data is retained for 12 months (see our privacy policy). There is no customer-facing audit log of organization activity or staff access.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-13-who-at-fly-io-can-access-our-machines-or-volumes-from-where-and-is-it-logged-or-disclosed-to-us) COMPLIANCE-13: Who at Fly.io can access our Machines or volumes, from where, and is it logged or disclosed to us?

**Restricted, logged, globally distributed.** Routine operations and security access is to hosts, not to the contents of your Machines, through IdP-backed certificate SSH with transcript-level audit, and does not require your consent. The contents of a Machine or volume are accessed only for security or maintenance, or for support with the owner’s consent, as stated in our privacy statement. Fly.io is a remote-first company with a globally distributed team and does not maintain or attest to a country-by-country list of personnel locations; personnel do not access platform infrastructure from countries subject to comprehensive US sanctions (Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria, and the Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk regions). If a disclosure form requires a positive country list, our public team page at fly.io/about shows a flag for each team member’s country; it is informational rather than a compliance record. Hosting providers’ personnel have physical access to hardware in the facility’s country; volumes are encrypted at rest with keys held by Fly.io. Access is logged internally and is not disclosed to the customer as a matter of course. Application secrets are encrypted by the control plane, which can only encrypt; plaintext exists only on the host at boot.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-14-what-is-your-breach-notification-timeframe) COMPLIANCE-14: What is your breach notification timeframe?

**Without undue delay.** Section 8 of the DPA commits us to notify you without undue delay after we or a sub-processor become aware of a personal data breach affecting your data, with the information required by GDPR Article 33(3): the nature of the breach and the categories and numbers of data subjects and records, a contact point, the likely consequences, and the measures taken. The standard DPA has no fixed hour count; fixed 24 or 72 hour commitments are available only under enterprise contracts.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-15-how-do-you-support-data-subject-requests-including-erasure) COMPLIANCE-15: How do you support data subject requests, including erasure?

**Self-service for account holders, DPA assistance for your end users.** Account holders edit their profile and delete their account themselves, from Account, then Settings, then Delete Account. Deletion is performed from inside the account, which is how we confirm that the request comes from the account holder, so we do not act on account or data deletion requests sent by email. Confirmation is shown on screen when the deletion completes; no confirmation email is sent. The profile and account data are removed within 30 days; invoices and billing records are retained for as long as tax and accounting law requires (DPA section 10.3). For data subjects in your applications we act as processor and assist you, the controller, under the DPA; those requests, and questions from people who do not hold a Fly.io account, go to [compliance@fly.io](mailto:compliance@fly.io).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-16-which-certifications-and-reports-can-you-provide-soc-2-iso-27001-pci-dss-hipaa-penetration-test) COMPLIANCE-16: Which certifications and reports can you provide (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA, penetration test)?

**SOC 2 Type 2 (Sept 2026), HIPAA BAA.** SOC 2 Type 2: our current report was issued on September 3, 2026 by Aprio LLP and covers August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 (Security and Confidentiality criteria). It is available under NDA from the Trust Center to organizations with the paid Compliance Package. The report describes the Fly.io platform; it does not name individual products such as Sprites, which run on the platform it covers, and Tigris is not a subservice organization in it. A bridge letter is not needed inside the first quarter after the audit period and is available on request after that. We do not hold ISO 27001, a PCI DSS AOC or FedRAMP, and none are planned; for datacenter ISO 27001 we can supply the facility operator’s certificate for the region you use. HIPAA: our BAA is self-service in the Trust Center for organizations with the paid Compliance Package (see COMPLIANCE-31), with a separate Tigris BAA for object storage. We do not distribute penetration test reports (see SOFTWARE-1); we provide an attestation letter and the SOC 2 report instead.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-17-which-products-does-the-baa-cover) COMPLIANCE-17: Which products does the BAA cover?

**Fly.io-operated services, including Sprites.** The Fly.io BAA is between your legal entity and Fly.io, Inc. and covers the protected health information Fly.io handles in connection with the services under the Terms of Service: Machines, volumes and volume snapshots, Managed Postgres including its backups, Sprites including their durable storage, secrets, networking and TLS termination, platform logs, and support access to your organization. Its scope is not itemized in the document, and no region or configuration is excluded. Where Fly.io uses another provider to deliver a covered service, that provider is our subcontractor under section 2.5 of the BAA and is bound to the same restrictions by a business associate agreement with us; this is how our hosting providers, AWS (encrypted snapshot and backup storage) and Tigris Data (durable storage behind Sprites) are covered, and you do not contract with them. Tigris therefore has two roles: it is on our sub-processor list for the storage behind Sprites, and nothing else. Your own Tigris object storage buckets and Upstash for Redis databases, even when provisioned and billed through Fly.io, are provided by Tigris Data and Upstash under their own terms (fly.io/legal/supplemental-terms), and those providers process your data as your processors directly, not as Fly.io sub-processors; neither the Fly.io DPA nor the Fly.io BAA covers them. The separate Tigris BAA in the Trust Center exists for that direct use of Tigris buckets and is signed by Tigris Data. Two practical limits: platform log lines and support ticket text can be processed by our AI sub-processors (COMPLIANCE-10), which are not under a BAA, so do not write PHI to standard output or paste it into support requests; and a BAA does not make an application HIPAA-compliant by itself, since the safeguards inside your application remain yours under the shared responsibility model.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-18-is-the-compliance-package-per-organization-and-is-the-soc-2-report-provided-per-organization) COMPLIANCE-18: Is the Compliance Package per organization, and is the SOC 2 report provided per organization?

**Package per org; DPA and BAA per entity.** The Compliance Package is purchased per organization, and the SOC 2 report is downloaded from that organization’s Trust Center under its NDA. The DPA and BAA are agreements between Fly.io and your legal entity, so once signed they cover every organization that entity owns; you request them from the Trust Center of one of your organizations (the BAA from one with the Compliance Package).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-19-can-we-process-special-category-data-for-example-health-data-or-payment-card-data-on-fly-io) COMPLIANCE-19: Can we process special-category data (for example health data) or payment card data on Fly.io?

**Yes, with a BAA for PHI.** There is no Terms of Service or Acceptable Use Policy restriction on special-category data on any plan; for PHI, sign the BAA (COMPLIANCE-17 and -31). A BAA covers Fly.io’s obligations as business associate; your application’s own HIPAA safeguards remain your responsibility. For card data, Fly.io does not hold a PCI DSS AOC. Controls such as PCI DSS 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 are application-level controls the merchant owns; our shared responsibility model and SOC 2 report cover the hosting layer.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-20-do-you-accept-custom-terms-audit-rights-breach-slas-sub-processor-pre-approval-liability) COMPLIANCE-20: Do you accept custom terms: audit rights, breach SLAs, sub-processor pre-approval, liability?

**Standard terms.** We contract on our standard terms. Section 11 of the DPA already provides audit rights: information reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance, and audits to the extent data protection law requires them. Anything beyond the standard DPA is enterprise contracting.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-21-will-you-sign-a-country-specific-cross-border-transfer-instrument-such-as-the-turkish-kvkk-standard-contract-kurul-standart-sozlesmesi) COMPLIANCE-21: Will you sign a country-specific cross-border transfer instrument, such as the Turkish KVKK standard contract (Kurul standart sözleşmesi)?

**No.** Fly.io executes one set of transfer instruments for every customer: the standard DPA, which incorporates the 2021 EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Module 2), together with our EU-US Data Privacy Framework certification including the UK Extension and the Swiss-US DPF. We do not sign country-specific instruments such as the Turkish Kurul standard contract, in any language or form, and we do not provide wet-ink counterparts, Turkish-language counterparts, or signatory-authority evidence for regulatory filings. Fly.io, Inc. is the only contracting entity; we have no EU-established affiliate available as a counterparty. Whether the standard instruments satisfy a customer’s local transfer law is a determination for the customer’s counsel.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-22-do-any-of-your-sub-processors-use-customer-data-to-train-or-improve-ai-ml-models) COMPLIANCE-22: Do any of your sub-processors use customer data to train or improve AI/ML models?

**Three exceptions, none with application content.** We reviewed the published terms of every sub-processor on fly.io/legal/sub-processors in October 2026. Those that hold support, account or operational data and offer AI features either commit in their terms not to train on customer data, or have had model training disabled at the account level (HubSpot and Slack, October 2026; our PostHog organization is on PostHog’s EU cloud, which is opted out of training by default; Sentry’s training opt-in is not enabled). The exceptions, none of which receive code, databases, application content or application logs, are: Stripe, which trains its fraud-prevention models on payment and transaction data as an independent controller, as it does for every merchant; Metronome, which may use de-identified usage billing events to improve its service; and Help Scout, which may use limited samples of support conversations to tune its own assistant features. There is no customer-level setting that changes these.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-23-in-which-countries-is-our-data-processed-including-edges-backups-and-remote-access) COMPLIANCE-23: In which countries is our data processed, including edges, backups and remote access?

**Your regions, plus the United States.** Application content, Machine memory and volumes are processed in the regions you deploy to; each region is a physical datacenter in the named city (see COMPLIANCE-6 and -7). Volume snapshots, the control plane, platform logs, metrics, proxy traces and image builds are processed in the United States regardless of region. Inbound TLS terminates at the Fly.io edge nearest the client: every region on fly.io/docs/reference/regions runs edge proxies, routing is BGP anycast with no separate failover list, and there is no per-app restriction on which edges accept traffic (see COMPLIANCE-8). Staff access is described in COMPLIANCE-13. The Location column on the sub-processor page is each vendor’s corporate location, not where your data is processed; for a given region only the hosting providers and AWS (snapshot storage) receive application content, and the remaining vendors hold account, billing, operational or support data.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-24-does-fly-io-or-its-infrastructure-use-covered-telecommunications-equipment-under-section-889-of-the-ndaa-huawei-zte-hytera-hikvision-dahua) COMPLIANCE-24: Does Fly.io or its infrastructure use covered telecommunications equipment under Section 889 of the NDAA (Huawei, ZTE, Hytera, Hikvision, Dahua)?

**No information of such use; no FAR representation.** Fly.io, Inc. is not a federal contractor and does not maintain a FAR 52.204-26 representation. Fly.io does not own or operate telecommunications or video surveillance equipment in any datacenter; we lease bare-metal servers from hosting providers who own and operate the facilities, network switching and routing, transit and physical security. Our inventory records identify the servers we lease as Supermicro, Gigabyte and Dell systems. We have no information indicating that equipment or services from Huawei, ZTE, Hytera, Hikvision, Dahua or their affiliates are used as a substantial or essential component of any system supporting the platform. We have not received or reviewed Section 889 representations from our hosting providers and cannot represent on their behalf.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-25-may-we-share-the-soc-2-report-with-our-auditors-or-consultants-store-it-in-a-compliance-platform-or-review-it-with-ai-tools) COMPLIANCE-25: May we share the SOC 2 report with our auditors or consultants, store it in a compliance platform, or review it with AI tools?

**Yes, within the NDA.** The NDA signed in the Trust Center permits access by your employees and authorized representatives who have a need to know and are bound by confidentiality obligations at least as restrictive as the NDA, which covers your CPA firm and compliance consultants, and permits reproduction as required for that purpose, which covers storing it as restricted evidence in a compliance platform such as Vanta. Reviewing the report with an AI tool is a disclosure to a third-party service; it is permitted where the account is on commercial terms under which the content is not used for training and is not retained beyond processing the request (for example the Anthropic API, Claude Team or Enterprise, the OpenAI API, Team or Enterprise); consumer accounts do not qualify. The PDF is the only format provided.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-26-may-we-run-a-penetration-test-or-security-scan-of-our-own-application-on-fly-io) COMPLIANCE-26: May we run a penetration test or security scan of our own application on Fly.io?

**Yes, with scope limits.** Yes. The Acceptable Use Policy’s security-testing restriction protects the platform and other tenants. You, or a security vendor acting for you, may run manual, non-volumetric application testing against your own apps, with no testing of Fly.io infrastructure or other tenants and no denial-of-service or volumetric testing. No advance notice to Fly.io is required. Written confirmation for a vendor’s authorization form is available from [compliance@fly.io](mailto:compliance@fly.io).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-27-which-categories-of-personal-data-may-we-process-on-fly-io-and-does-the-dpa-exclude-any) COMPLIANCE-27: Which categories of personal data may we process on Fly.io, and does the DPA exclude any?

**No excluded categories.** The DPA does not exclude any category of personal data. Annex I.B defines the categories transferred as those you elect to provide, so financial details, payroll and employee records, and documents containing them are within scope once described there. Clause 8.7 of the embedded Standard Contractual Clauses applies additional safeguards only to “sensitive data” as defined (racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, trade union membership, genetic and biometric data, health, sex life, criminal convictions), which you record in Annex I.B. For PHI, sign the BAA (COMPLIANCE-19).

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-28-how-do-we-complete-the-dpa-template-and-what-if-a-field-is-cut-off-in-the-signed-copy) COMPLIANCE-28: How do we complete the DPA template, and what if a field is cut off in the signed copy?

**Signature page and Annex I fields; confirmation on request.** You complete the signature page (company legal name, signer name, title, date), the Annex I.A data exporter block (name, address, contact person, activities relevant to the transfer; the role is prefilled as Controller), and two Annex I.B fields: “Sensitive data transferred” (write “None” if no Clause 8.7 categories are involved) and “The frequency of the transfer” (typically “Continuous”). Signing through Dropbox Sign executes the agreement; nothing needs to be returned by email, and the “how to execute” text on page 1 predates the dashboard flow. The form’s text fields have a length limit; if an entry is cut off in the completed PDF, tell us the intended text and we confirm it in writing against the executed record. The executed copy stays as signed and is downloadable from the Trust Center.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-29-we-are-outside-the-eu-uk-for-example-south-africa-turkiye-brazil-which-transfer-provisions-apply-to-us) COMPLIANCE-29: We are outside the EU/UK (for example South Africa, Türkiye, Brazil). Which transfer provisions apply to us?

**Same DPA; SCCs where your law requires them.** The DPA defines Data Protection Laws to include the privacy laws of any country, and a Restricted Transfer as any transfer that would be prohibited without the Standard Contractual Clauses; where that applies, Section 12 enters the parties into the Module 2 Clauses in Annex 2. The Data Privacy Framework certification covers data of EU, UK and Swiss origin only. We do not execute country-specific instruments (see COMPLIANCE-21) and do not opine on whether the standard instruments satisfy your local law; that is a determination for you and your counsel. Your own transfer from your country to the Fly.io region you choose is yours as controller.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-30-can-you-confirm-our-accepted-agreement-version-and-acceptance-date) COMPLIANCE-30: Can you confirm our accepted agreement version and acceptance date?

**Terms of Service, accepted at account creation.** Use of the platform is governed by the Terms of Service at fly.io/legal/terms-of-service as in effect, accepted when the account is created. We do not record a separate per-account terms version or acceptance timestamp; the account creation date is the acceptance date. Self-service accounts have no order forms or amendments. Executed DPA, BAA and NDA copies are downloadable from the Trust Center of the organization that signed them.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-31-how-do-we-get-a-baa-what-does-it-cost-and-can-we-see-it-before-buying) COMPLIANCE-31: How do we get a BAA, what does it cost, and can we see it before buying?

**Compliance Package, $99/month, self-service.** The BAA is included in the Compliance Package, a $99 per month add-on purchased per organization from the Trust Center in the dashboard. It is billed monthly on a Pay As You Go organization with no annual commitment and no spend commitment; organizations on legacy plans create a Pay As You Go organization to buy it. Once the package is active, an organization admin requests the BAA from the Trust Center, it arrives pre-signed by Fly.io, Inc. through Dropbox Sign, and it takes effect when you sign. The executed copy is then downloadable from the same page. The package also unlocks the SOC 2 report under NDA. The DPA is free on every plan and does not require the package. Reviewing the terms before you commit: COMPLIANCE-17, 32 and 33 summarise what the BAA covers and its notification, subcontractor and termination terms, and the full text is shown in the Dropbox Sign request before anything is signed; if it does not suit, cancel the package for a prorated refund. We do not circulate unsigned copies by email as a matter of course. We sign only our own BAA; customer paper, shorter breach-notice windows and other custom terms are enterprise contracting.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-32-what-are-the-baas-breach-notification-subcontractor-and-termination-terms) COMPLIANCE-32: What are the BAA’s breach notification, subcontractor and termination terms?

**30 days from discovery; return or destroy on termination.** Breach notification: section 2.4.1 of the BAA commits Fly.io to report a Breach of Unsecured PHI to you within thirty (30) calendar days of discovery, with the information required by 45 CFR 164.410, and section 5.2.3 to report Security Incidents. This is the BAA’s own term and is separate from the DPA’s “without undue delay” (COMPLIANCE-14). Subcontractors: section 2.5 requires any subcontractor that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI on our behalf to agree to the same restrictions; our hosting providers and AWS are listed at fly.io/legal/sub-processors. Termination: the BAA runs until terminated under section 7 (for cause after a cure period, or when all PHI has been returned or destroyed). On termination, section 7.3 provides for return of PHI to you or, if you agree, destruction, with protections extended to any PHI that cannot feasibly be returned. Deleting your apps, volumes and organization is the self-service route to destruction; residual encrypted backups age out within 90 days (COMPLIANCE-11). Cancelling the Compliance Package does not by itself terminate an executed BAA; it ends under its own terms.

### [Anchor](https://fly.io/legal/security-questionnaire/\#compliance-33-we-signed-the-baa-on-the-wrong-organization-or-under-the-wrong-entity-name-or-need-a-copy-of-an-old-one-what-now) COMPLIANCE-33: We signed the BAA on the wrong organization, or under the wrong entity name, or need a copy of an old one. What now?

**BAA binds the entity; package is per org.** The BAA binds the legal entity named on its signature page to Fly.io, Inc.; it is not tied to a particular organization, so it covers every organization that entity owns and an organization rename does not affect it. The Compliance Package, by contrast, is a per-organization subscription and cannot be moved: if it was bought on the wrong organization, cancel it there for a prorated refund and buy it on the right one. If the entity name was entered incorrectly or cut off by the form’s field limit, write to [compliance@fly.io](mailto:compliance@fly.io): we confirm the intended name in writing against the executed record, or send a replacement BAA for signature while the executed one stays in force. Executed copies of documents signed since August 2026 are downloadable from the Trust Center of the organization that signed them; for older ones, [compliance@fly.io](mailto:compliance@fly.io) retrieves the Dropbox Sign record.
